summary: Specifies the Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP), which manages joint or exclusive access to shared resources in a multiparty conference. Floor control complements the protocols that handle session setup and conference policy. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: In a group meeting, only one person should speak at a time. This protocol is like a talking stick that decides who gets to use something shared, such as the screen or the microphone.

questions: how does floor control work in conferencing
how does bfcp floor control work
does bfcp use tcp or udp
subtitle: A talking stick for conferences: how participants ask for, hold and give up shared resources like the right to send video.

tldr.problem: In a multiparty conference, some shared resources, such as the right to send media into a particular session, must be handed out in a coordinated way, either to one user at a time or to several.
tldr.mechanism: BFCP is a compact binary protocol in which floor participants send requests to a floor control server, floor chairs tell the server what to decide, and the server reports status back. It runs over TCP with TLS or over UDP with DTLS.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 4582 and adds support for UDP as an unreliable transport, new message types, retransmission timers and fragmentation. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Transports
facts.value: TCP with TLS, UDP with DTLS

today: RFC 8855 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It obsoletes RFC 4582 and is paired with RFC 8856, which defines how to describe BFCP streams in SDP. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata.

sections.title: What Floor Control Is For
sections.content:
Within a conference, some applications need to manage access to a set of shared resources, such as the right to send media to a particular media session. Floor control gives users coordinated, shared or exclusive access to those resources. A floor is a temporary permission to access or manipulate a specific shared resource or set of resources.

The Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) meets the requirements the RFC cites for floor control protocols. It is also designed for low-bandwidth environments: the binary encoding keeps messages small, which matters for delay-sensitive messages such as FloorRequest, FloorRelease, FloorRequestStatus and ChairAction.

The RFC is explicit about scope. BFCP only arbitrates access to floors. Creating floors, tying them to resources such as media streams, and the rules for deciding who gets them are handled by other protocols, such as the conference control protocol that manipulates the conference object.
sections.eli5: When many people share one thing, like a single microphone, someone has to decide whose turn it is. BFCP is just the way people ask and get told, not the rules for choosing.

sections.title: Roles and Concepts
sections.content:
The protocol has three main roles. A floor participant requests floors and may ask for information about them. A floor chair is a moderator that manages one floor by granting, denying or revoking it. The floor control server keeps the state of the floors: which floors exist, who the chairs are and who holds each floor. A client is either a participant or a chair talking to the server over BFCP.

Roles are defined transaction by transaction, so one entity can be a participant in one exchange and a chair in another. A media participant is an entity that has access to the conference media. It is usually co-located with a floor participant but does not need to be, which enables third-party floor requests, where one participant requests a floor for another.

Holding a floor gives the right to use the associated resources, for example the right to send media over a particular audio stream. It does not by itself stop others from physically using those resources; that is discussed in the XCON Framework.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of people: the kid who asks for the stick, the teacher's helper who says yes or no, and the teacher's notebook that remembers who has it. A friend can also ask for the stick on your behalf.

sections.title: How a Floor Request Plays Out
sections.content:
A participant asks for a floor by sending a FloorRequest carrying one or more FLOOR-ID attributes. If several floors are listed, the server treats them as an atomic package: it either grants all of them or denies all of them.

The server answers with FloorRequestStatus messages. The first one is the response and carries the same Transaction ID as the request, plus a Floor Request ID that identifies the request from then on. Later status messages reuse that ID. In the RFC's example the request moves from Pending to Accepted to Granted, and a later FloorRelease ends it with a Released status.

Pending means the server needs to contact a chair to accept the request but has not yet done so; once the chair accepts, it is Accepted. The server is ultimately responsible for keeping coherent floor state and treats ChairAction instructions as input, not as commands it must perform exactly. For example, it will not grant one floor of an atomic request until the chairs of the other floors agree, and it may need to revoke a floor from its current holder first.

Participants and chairs can also query the server with FloorQuery, FloorRequestQuery and UserQuery, and a Hello message lets a client learn which attributes and primitives the server supports.
sections.eli5: You raise your hand and the teacher writes down your place in line. You get told when you are next and when you finally have the stick. If a friend is waiting for two things at once, they get both or neither.

sections.title: The Binary Message Format
sections.content:
Every BFCP packet is a 12-octet COMMON-HEADER followed by attributes, all in network byte order. The header carries a 3-bit version, an R flag and an F flag, a 3-bit reserved field, an 8-bit primitive, a 16-bit payload length (in 4-octet units, excluding the header), a 32-bit conference ID, a 16-bit transaction ID and a 16-bit user ID. Two optional 16-bit fields, Fragment Offset and Fragment Length, appear only when F is set, which never happens on reliable transports.

The version is 1 over a reliable transport and 2 over an unreliable one. The RFC recommends choosing the conference ID randomly, because predictable IDs on a nonsecure transport make off-path injection of forged messages possible.

Attributes use a TLV (Type-Length-Value) encoding, aligned to 32 bits. A 7-bit type is followed by an M (mandatory) bit and an 8-bit length. Attribute formats are Unsigned16, OctetString16, OctetString and Grouped (an attribute containing attributes). Eighteen attribute types are defined, from BENEFICIARY-ID (1) to OVERALL-REQUEST-STATUS (18). An unrecognized attribute with the M bit set makes the server send an Error with code 4; one without it is ignored.

Seventeen primitives are defined, from FloorRequest (1) to GoodbyeAck (17). Request statuses are Pending, Accepted, Granted, Denied, Cancelled, Released and Revoked. Priority runs from 0 (Lowest) to 4 (Highest), with 2 (Normal) as the default.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with a small label saying what kind of message it is and which meeting it belongs to. After the label come little labelled boxes of details, each saying how big it is.

sections.title: Transports, Transactions and Timers
sections.content:
Two transports are supported: TCP where connectivity is not impeded by NATs or media relays, and UDP where TCP may not be applicable. Over TCP a client must not use more than one connection to a given floor control server within a conference, and an entity that receives unparseable data must close the connection. Reconnection attempts should not happen more than once in a 30 second period.

Over UDP each datagram holds exactly one message or fragment. Clients announce themselves with Hello and consider the server available only after HelloAck. An entity may have at most one outstanding request transaction per peer, which limits congestion and reordering. Ending a connection requires a Goodbye. ICMP messages must be ignored because of off-path attack risk.

Client-initiated transactions are a request and a response. Server-initiated ones are single notifications with Transaction ID 0 over a reliable transport, but over UDP they are request and acknowledgement pairs with non-zero, monotonically increasing IDs. Timer T1 retransmits requests, starting at 500 ms, doubling on each retry and failing after three unacknowledged retransmissions, after which the connection is considered broken. Timer T2, set to (T1*2^(4))*1.25, controls how long a response is cached.

Messages larger than the path MTU are fragmented by BFCP itself rather than by IP. Individual fragments are not acknowledged; the whole message is acknowledged once complete. For NAT traversal over UDP, the RFC recommends STUN Binding Indication keepalives and symmetric ports.
sections.eli5: BFCP can send its notes by a careful courier who checks that every note arrived, or by a quick mail slot with no guarantee. For the mail slot, it re-sends a note if nobody answers, waiting longer each time, and gives up after a few tries.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
BFCP relies on lower-layer security for replay and integrity protection and confidentiality. Entities must support TLS over TCP and DTLS over UDP. For backward compatibility with RFC 4582 they must support at least the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA cipher suite, and they should also support four ECDHE or DHE suites with AES-GCM.

Clients should authenticate the floor control server, and servers should authenticate clients. If the signaling used to set up the conference is itself authenticated and protected, authentication becomes mandatory. TLS/DTLS mutual authentication is the recommended mechanism, relying on an initial integrity-protected channel to exchange certificates (which may be self-signed) or their fingerprints. A server that receives plain messages may reply with Error code 9 (Use TLS) or 11 (Use DTLS).

Authentication is not enough on its own: the server must also authorize each message, and must check that the User ID on an authenticated connection is one that connection's user may use. Otherwise it generates Error code 5 (Unauthorized Operation).

The security considerations walk through impersonating a client, impersonating a server, modifying messages, replaying messages and eavesdropping, and attribute each defense to TLS/DTLS plus the User ID check. To make denial-of-service with spoofed addresses harder, the RFC says entities should use the DTLS cookie exchange.
sections.eli5: Before the stick is handed out, everyone shows ID, and the whole conversation happens in a locked room so nobody can listen in or pretend to be the teacher.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 4582
sections.content:
The main purpose of this revision was to support BFCP over an unreliable transport. That brought the version value 2, the R and F flags, the optional fragment fields, four new primitives (FloorRequestStatusAck, FloorStatusAck, Goodbye, GoodbyeAck), new error codes (Unable to Parse Message, Use DTLS, Unsupported Version), a transport section split into reliable and unreliable parts, mandatory DTLS for UDP, and the T1 and T2 timers.

Other fixes include two more error codes (Incorrect Message Length and Generic Error), additional recommended cipher suites, ABNF notation cleanups, and tighter normative language, with several SHOULDs changed to MUSTs. Appendix A gives example call flows over an unreliable transport, and Appendix B explains the motivation for it.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook only worked with the careful courier. This new edition adds rules for the quick mail slot too, and tidies up some unclear sentences.

fields.name: Ver
fields.desc: Version: 1 over reliable transport, 2 over unreliable.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Transaction Responder flag; used only over unreliable transport.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Fragmentation flag; used only over unreliable transport.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Message length in 4-octet units, excluding the header.

fields.name: Transaction ID
fields.desc: Matches a message with its response.

fields.name: User ID
fields.desc: Identifies a participant within the conference.
